newsitem.title: UK: Grobbelaar scared about fixing matches - witness.
newsitem.headline: Grobbelaar scared about fixing matches - witness.

text.p: Former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, on trial accused of match fixing, became increasingly worried about the risks posed by rigging soccer games as time went on, a court heard on Tuesday.

Prosecution witness Chris Vincent, a business partner of Grobbelaar's until the two men fell out, played tapes to the court that prosecutors said showed the Zimbabwean-born player was getting anxious about taking money to throw games.
"When I had my first meeting with Grobbelaar he had mentioned that it was too dangerous at the moment to consider fixing matches," Vincent testified.

Prosecutors are trying to prove that Grobbelaar and three others were involved in a match-rigging scheme involving an Asian betting syndicate. After a business deal went sour in June 1994 Vincent went to the Sun newspaper, which helped him organise a tape-recorded sting against the player involving a second, non-existent syndicate.
The jury of nine men and three women has been shown a videotape recorded using a hidden camera that shows Vincent meeting Grobbelaar in the room of a Southampton hotel.
The prosecution alleges Grobbelaar accepted 2,000 pounds ($3,300) from Vincent.
Vincent said Grobbelaar decided to fix games because he was unhappy at being paid less than others in the Liverpool team.
In the tape, Grobbelaar says he is interested in the idea of the mythical syndicate but asks Vincent -- who promised not to name names -- to scout around and come up with more details.
"There are investigators all around. I don't know that these aren't investigators," he said.

Former striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim -- who the prosecution and Vincent say was the syndicate middleman whom Grobbelaar referred to as the "Short Man" -- are also on trial on match-fixing charges. Also on trial is former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers, accused with Lim and Fashanu of taking part in a separate bid to fix matches.All four accused have pleaded not guilty.
Vincent told the court that in October 1994 he was surprised to hear that Lim was back in the picture -- and Grobbelaar apparently fixing matches again.
"We were playing snooker. He received a call on his mobile telephone and talked for a bit," Vincent told the court.
"At the end of the conversation he said, quote, "do you know who that was?' I said no. He said, quote, "That was the short man. He's talking about this weekend'."

The tapes were often unintelligible and Vincent was frequently prompted to re-state to the court what was on them. "You don't have to do anything for six months or so," Vincent could be heard telling Grobbelaar on the tape. "It's too dangerous but I'll look at it," Grobbelaar replied.
